## References

1. [EnvScaler: Scaling Tool-Interactive Environments for LLM Agent via Programmatic Synthesis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.05808)
2. Code: [RUC-NLPIR/EnvScaler @ 96ae8b0](https://github.com/RUC-NLPIR/EnvScaler)

# Notes

## The problem: you cannot train an agent without somewhere for it to act

Picture the job a customer-service agent does in [[2406.12045 - Tau-Bench (Tool-Agent-User Interaction)]]. A user says "cancel the bookshelf and the jigsaw puzzle, they came in different orders." The agent has to ask for an email, look up the user, find both orders, check that each item is still cancellable under the store's rules, and then call the right tool with the right IDs. Every one of those tool calls reads or changes a database, and the next step depends on what came back.

To teach a model to do this well, you need many places where it can practice: a database it can read and change, a set of tools, rules about what is allowed, a task, and a way to tell afterwards whether the task got done. The paper calls such a place a tool-interactive environment. The authors' bet is that a model which has practised in many different environments will handle an environment it has never seen.

There are three ways to get such environments, and each fails somewhere.

1. **Real systems** (a real airline backend). Realistic, but you usually cannot get access, and you cannot reset them or run thousands of copies.
2. **An LLM pretending to be the environment.** You describe the system and let a model make up tool results. This scales, but the model forgets what it said two calls ago, invents records, and returns results that contradict each other. [[2511.01824 - Simia Simulating Environments with Reasoning Models for Agent Training]] is the main recent example of this route, and it is cited here as the thing to avoid.
3. **Hand-written programs** (BFCL, τ-bench, ToolSandbox). Each environment is Python code with real state, so it is consistent and reproducible. But people wrote these by hand to use as benchmarks, and there are only a handful.

EnvScaler takes the third route and automates it. The LLM does not pretend to be the environment. It writes the environment's code once, and from then on the code runs the environment. That one change is what the paper's Table 1 is about: programs give you consistency, control, stability and inspectability, and the automation gives you scale.

The paper also places itself against two closer relatives. Some prior work models only the tools as separate functions, with no shared database behind them, so calling `send_message` never changes what `list_messages` returns. Other work (AgentScaler, AutoForge) needs a collection of tools or tool documentation to start from. EnvScaler starts from plain task text and nothing else.

## What an "environment" is here

The paper writes an environment as three things, $E = \{F_{exec}, E_{doc}, \Sigma_{tool}\}$:

- $F_{exec}$ is one Python class. Its attributes are the database (for example `self.users`, `self.messages`, each a dict from ID to record). Its methods are the tools. Calling a method reads or edits those dicts.
- $E_{doc}$ is the text the agent sees about the environment: a short introduction plus the business rules ("returns only when the item status is Delivered").
- $\Sigma_{tool}$ is the list of tool names, parameters and descriptions the agent is allowed to call. These are pulled out of the class's method signatures.

This "a class is the environment" shape matters for everything later. The full state is just the object's attributes, so you can snapshot it, compare it before and after a call, and hand it to a checking function.

## Stage 1 — SkelBuilder: building the environment's code

SkelBuilder produces the skeleton: the class with its state and tools, with no data in it yet. It has three steps.

### 1a. Finding what environments to build, by reading old tasks

You need a list of environment topics, and you want it diverse. Instead of writing the list by hand or deriving it from an API catalogue, the authors read it out of existing instruction datasets. A task like "notify Bob about the evacuation" implies that a messaging app exists somewhere with contacts and a message history. A task like "Tom had 180 apples and gave away 75%" implies no environment at all.

So an LLM $M$ first answers a strict yes/no question for each task $t$: does this task need a domain-specific system with persistent state that you can both read and change? For every "yes", it writes a description of the most plausible environment:

$$\{E'_{des}\} = \{M(P^{env}_{infer} \| t) \mid t \in T_{exist}, M(P^{task}_{filter} \| t)\}$$

Read it as: for each task in the existing set, if the filter prompt says yes, run the inference prompt on it and collect the resulting description. The $\|$ just means "prompt text followed by the task text." The descriptions are then embedded and near-duplicates are dropped, giving a non-redundant set $\{E_{des}\}$. The source tasks were API-Bank and ToolACE, chosen because many of their tasks survive the filter.

The inference prompt (Figure 13) also asks the model to score each environment on "Usefulness" and "Modelability", where Modelability means how easily it can be written as one Python class. That second score is a quiet design choice: the pipeline favours environments that fit its own single-class shape.

### 1b. Plan first, then write code piece by piece

Going from a one-paragraph description straight to a 500-line class fails often. So the authors split it.

**Planning.** From the description, the LLM writes the state (entities and their attributes, such as `User: _id, phone_number, name`) and the rules. Then, given all of that, it lists the tool operations, split into read-only queries and state-changing operations:

$$E_{state}, E_{rule} = M(P^{state}_{plan} \| E_{des}), \quad \{E_{tool_i}\} = M(P^{tool}_{plan} \| E_{des} \| E_{state} \| E_{rule})$$

The rules are appended to the description to form $E_{doc}$, which is what the agent will later read.

**Coding.** The LLM first turns the state plan into class attributes $F_{attr}$ (TypedDicts plus an `__init__`). Then it writes each tool method separately, each time given the rules, the attributes and that one tool's description:

$$F_{attr} = M(P^{state}_{exec} \| E_{state}), \quad F_{meth_i} = M(P^{tool}_{exec} \| E_{rule} \| F_{attr} \| E_{tool_i})$$

Writing one method at a time with the same attribute definitions in view is what keeps the methods consistent with each other: they all read and write the same dicts.

**Assembly.** The pieces are merged into one file, $F_{exec} = \text{Merge}(F_{attr}, \{F_{meth_i}\})$. The file is parsed with Python's AST (the parser that checks whether code is valid Python); files that fail are thrown away. The method signatures, pulled out by AST plus regex, become $\Sigma_{tool}$.

The result is large: on average 18.58 tools per environment (10.44 queries, 8.14 state changes), 21.38 state fields, and 4.58 rules.

### 1c. Testing the code with two agents

Code that parses is not code that works. The obvious fix, asking an LLM to read the code and score it, judges code by how it looks. The authors instead run the code and judge what it actually did.

- A **testing agent** $M_{test}$ sees only what a user of the environment would see: the tool list and the current state $S_j$. It does not see the source. Each round it proposes one call: $call_j = M_{test}(\Sigma_{tool}, S_j)$. Some calls are meant to succeed ("positive") and some are meant to be rejected ("negative"), such as deleting a file that does not exist.
- The environment runs the call: $R_j, S_{j+1} = \text{Exec}(F_{meth}, call_j, S_j)$.
- A **checking agent** $M_{check}$ sees everything: the method's source, the return value $R_j$, and the state difference $\Delta S_{j \to j+1}$. It rules Pass, Warning or Fail.

This split is the clever part. The tester behaves like an outside user, so it finds the cases a real agent will hit. The checker has the source code and the state difference, so it can tell "the method said success but nothing changed in the database" apart from real success. That is exactly the inconsistency that sinks LLM-simulated environments.

After $N$ rounds, the score is the average verdict:

$$score_{env} = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{j=1}^{N} judge_j$$

$N = 100$, and environments below 0.85 are thrown away. Of 266 generated environments, 191 survived, so 28.2% were rejected. When they classified the failed test cases (using Claude-4.5-Sonnet), the largest groups were type errors (31.9%) and attribute errors (25.1%), then state inconsistency (18.1%) and logic errors (15.6%). So most failures are ordinary code bugs, not the model misunderstanding the domain.

As a separate check, Claude-4.5-Sonnet scored the 191 survivors on three 1-10 scales: does each tool's code match its description (8.58), does it behave correctly (8.97), and does it handle bad input (8.60).

## Stage 2 — ScenGenerator: filling the environment with work

A skeleton is an empty database with tools. To train on it you need data in the database, a task, and a way to score the agent's attempt. ScenGenerator makes these, and makes many per environment: about 37 on average, about 7K in total.

### Data first, then the task

The order matters. A task has to be solvable from the data that exists: you cannot ask the agent to cancel order #4512 if there is no order #4512. So the LLM first writes the initial state as JSON, given the class and state schema: $S_{init} = M(P^{gen}_{init} \| F_{exec} \| E_{state})$. Only then does it write a task grounded in that state and the rules: $task = M(P^{gen}_{task} \| S_{init} \| E_{tool} \| E_{rule})$.

The authors deliberately avoid a common alternative, used by AgentScaler and AutoForge: randomly chain tool calls, then ask an LLM to invent the task that would produce that chain. They give two reasons. Tasks invented backwards from random chains tend to be low quality. And a task usually has several correct solutions, so treating one tool chain as the single right answer punishes an agent that solves it another valid way.

### Scoring by checking the final database, not the steps

That second reason drives the scoring design. Instead of comparing the agent's tool calls with a reference sequence, EnvScaler looks only at the database after the agent finishes.

1. An LLM breaks the task into a checklist of independent yes/no items, each starting with "Has ...". For example: "Has the contact 'Jade Williams' with number 5036481912 been created for USER2?"
2. For each item $c_k$, the LLM writes a Python function `check_func(final_state)` that returns True or False.
3. After the agent finishes, every function runs on the final state. The reward is the fraction that pass:

$$reward = \frac{1}{K}\sum_{k=1}^{K} \mathbb{1}[f_{c_k}(S_{final}) = \text{True}]$$

Symbol by symbol: $K$ is the number of checklist items; $f_{c_k}$ is the generated function for item $k$; $S_{final}$ is the environment's state when the episode ends; $\mathbb{1}[\cdot]$ is 1 if the condition holds and 0 otherwise. So the reward is a number from 0 to 1.

Why this is better than one "did it succeed?" check: it gives partial credit (an agent that did 6 of 8 things gets 0.75, not 0), and a small single-condition function is easier for an LLM to write correctly than one function that checks everything. Why this is better than matching steps: any path that ends in the right database state scores the same. This is the "verifier" layer of [[four-layer-scoring-stack-for-rl-environments]], built automatically, and it is the same idea as [[execution-based-tool-evaluation]]: check the outcome, not the form of the call.

The weak point is that the checker is LLM-written code that nothing validates before training uses it. [[llm-generated-reward-programs-need-validation]] describes exactly this risk for Patronus's generative simulators, and it applies here too (see the code section: a failed function simply counts as a failed check forever).

### Is the synthetic task set hard enough?

On 50 sampled scenarios, Qwen3-4B without thinking scores 37.53, Qwen3-8B with thinking scores 57.78, and the 30B teacher scores 67.07. Episodes run about 15 steps without a user and over 25 with one. Stronger models win more head-to-head comparisons, which is evidence that the checks separate good agents from weak ones. One surprising number: the best of 8 samples from Qwen3-8B scores 69.38, higher than a single try from the 30B model. There is a lot of reward to find by trying again, which is what RL needs.

## Training: two ways to talk to the environment

The paper frames an episode as a partially observable decision process. The agent never sees the database directly; it sees only its history of actions and results: $a_t = \pi_\theta(H_t, o_t)$ and $o_{t+1}, S_{t+1} = E(a_t, S_t)$. Here $\pi_\theta$ is the model, $H_t$ is the history, $o_t$ is the latest observation, and $S_t$ is the hidden database.

There are two settings:

- **Non-Conversation.** The agent gets the whole task at once and calls tools until it says it is done or hits the step limit.
- **Conversation.** An LLM plays the user and reveals the task bit by bit (the user prompt forbids giving all sub-tasks or all details at once). The agent has one extra action, talking to the user. The episode ends when the simulated user says the task is done. This is the τ-bench style, and it adds the simulator-error concern from [[llm-user-simulator-design-and-auditing]].

**Split.** 140 environments go to SFT and a separate 51 to RL. For SFT, Qwen3-30B-A3B-Thinking plays the agent in both settings, giving about 9K trajectories. A detail worth knowing: Qwen3's chat template deletes the reasoning from earlier turns. So a trajectory with $n$ turns is split into $n$ training samples, and in each only the last turn's reasoning and action are trained on. Otherwise the model would only ever learn to reason in the final turn.

For RL they use Reinforce++ in the Non-Conversation setting: 64 tasks per step, 8 attempts each, KL coefficient 0.1 (the KL term keeps the model close to where it started), up to 200 steps. See [[Cameron R. Wolfe - GRPO Tricks (Making RL Actually Work)]] for how group-sampled RL like this works.

## Results

Evaluation uses three multi-turn tool benchmarks that the training never touched: BFCL-v3 Multi-Turn (8 environments such as a file system and vehicle control), τ-Bench (retail and airline), and ACEBench-Agent.

Overall scores (Table 4), base → +SFT → +SFT & RL:

- **Qwen3-8B:** BFCL-MT 28.88 → 37.00 → 41.88; τ-Bench 38.19 → 41.35 → 44.81; ACEBench 60.00 → 71.67 → 72.50.
- **Qwen3-4B:** BFCL-MT 25.38 → 34.88 → 38.00; τ-Bench 33.44 → 38.20 → 41.06; ACEBench 55.28 → 66.67 → 70.55.
- **Qwen3-1.7B:** BFCL-MT 9.75 → 18.13 → 23.00; τ-Bench 12.50 → 17.44 → 16.28; ACEBench 31.95 → 43.61 → 50.00.

For scale, GPT-4.1 scores 40.00 on BFCL-MT, 57.48 on τ-Bench and 77.50 on ACEBench. So the trained 8B model beats GPT-4.1 on BFCL-MT but is still far behind on τ-Bench.

Three patterns are worth understanding:

1. **SFT helps every model; RL helps big models more.** RL moves 8B up on every benchmark, but 1.7B loses a little on τ-Bench after RL. The authors' explanation: a small model explores badly and is more easily misled by noisy rewards, so what it learns does not transfer.
2. **τ-Bench gains are the smallest.** τ-Bench is mostly about reasoning under strict policy rules (airline change fees, what you may refund). EnvScaler's environments have about 4.6 rules each, and its tasks are mainly about using many tools across many steps. So it teaches the tool-use part more than the rule-following part. The 1.7B model does worse on τ-Bench Airline after training (16.00 → 14.00).
3. **Gains track breadth, not closeness to the test set.** This is the most interesting analysis. They measured how similar each training environment is to the BFCL environments (by embedding its topic and tool descriptions) and trained Qwen3-4B on the most similar half, the least similar half, or a random half. The overall scores were 32.00, 32.50 and 31.25, all far above the 25.38 base. If the gains came from training on look-alikes of the test set, the similar half would win. It does not. What transfers is the general skill of working with tools across many steps.

Related to that, more environments help, with the steepest gain from 0 to 20 environments and slower but continued gains up to 141.

**What each interaction style teaches (Table 6, Qwen3-8B on BFCL-MT).** Training only without a user is best when the task is fully stated (Base 49.50). Training only with a user is best when a parameter is missing and the agent must ask for it (Miss-Param 30.50 versus 23.50). Training on both gives the best overall score (37.00). No setting improves Miss-Func, where a needed tool is absent, because the training data has no tasks where a tool is missing. The model cannot learn to notice a missing tool if it never met one.

**RL alone, without SFT first (Table 7).** Every model improves, but less than SFT then RL. There is one detail the paper does not stress: for Qwen3-8B, RL alone on 51 environments raises BFCL-MT to 37.62, about the same as SFT alone (37.00), and τ-Bench to 42.30, slightly above SFT alone (41.35). On ACEBench, SFT alone is well ahead (71.67 versus 63.05). So for a capable model, trial and error in the synthetic environments gives about as much as copying 9K teacher trajectories on two of the three benchmarks.

**Without reasoning (Appendix C.1, Qwen3-4B).** They compare against two public datasets. APIGen (60K single-turn examples) makes things worse on every benchmark: single-turn practice does not teach multi-turn tool use. APIGen-MT (5K multi-turn examples from the same two domains as τ-Bench) raises τ-Bench by 13.78 but lowers BFCL-MT, because it trains the model to chat with the user before using tools. EnvScaler adds 11.00 on BFCL-MT and 11.11 on ACEBench but loses 1.58 on τ-Bench. This is the clearest evidence in the paper that breadth transfers while domain-matched data does not.

**Cost.** About $1 per environment (most of it the 100-round two-agent test) and about $0.06 per scenario, using GPT-4.1 and GPT-4.1-mini.

## How the code implements it

The repo is the full pipeline: `skel_builder/` (Stage 1), `scen_generator/` (Stage 2), `interact_with_env/` (the environment wrappers for data collection and evaluation), plus SFT (LlamaFactory) and RL (a copy of the ROLL framework).

### 1. The reward: run each generated check, average the results

**Problem.** After an episode, turn the final database into one number using the checklist functions.

`interact_with_env/envscaler_env/base_env.py:282-303 @ 96ae8b0`
```python
    def calculate_reward(self, checklist_with_func: list, init_state: dict, pred_final_state: dict) -> float:
        """Calculate reward based on final state."""
        checklist_with_func_result = []

        for check_item in checklist_with_func:
            check_func_str = check_item["check_func"]
            success, result, error = run_check_function(
                func_code=check_func_str,
                init_state=init_state,
                final_state=pred_final_state
            )
            new_check_item = deepcopy(check_item)
            new_check_item["check_func_result"] = {"success": success, "result": result, "error": error}
            checklist_with_func_result.append(new_check_item)

        check_avg_result = round(
            sum([item["check_func_result"]["result"] for item in checklist_with_func_result if item["check_func_result"]["result"] is not None])
            / len(checklist_with_func_result),
            4
        )

        return check_avg_result
```

**Walkthrough.** This is the paper's reward equation. Each check is stored as a string of code, run against the final state, and the True/False results are summed (True counts as 1) and divided by the number of checks. Note the difference between the numerator and the denominator. A check whose code crashes or returns something other than a boolean has `result = None`, so it is left out of the sum but still counted in `len(...)`. A broken check therefore acts as a check the agent always fails. This is the cautious choice (a broken check can never give free reward), but it also means a scenario with one broken check can never score 1.0. Also, `gen_check_func` returns an empty string if it fails to parse the LLM's output five times, and an empty string always fails this way. Nothing in `scen_generator/` runs the checks against any reference final state before they are used, so the paper's "rule-based" reward is only as good as the unchecked LLM-written functions.

### 2. Running LLM-written code as the judge

**Problem.** Check functions are code strings produced by an LLM. They must be run, given access to the initial state, and kept from crashing the trainer.

`interact_with_env/envscaler_env/utils/env_util.py:102-127 @ 96ae8b0`
```python
def run_check_function(func_code: str, init_state: dict, final_state: dict):
    """
    Dynamically execute a verification function defined in func_code.
    """
    safe_globals = {
        '__builtins__': __builtins__,
    }
    safe_globals.update({"initial_state": deepcopy(init_state)})

    try:
        # Execute in safe_globals, function will retain this global scope
        exec(func_code, safe_globals)

        if 'check_func' not in safe_globals:
            return False, None, "Function 'check_func' not found."

        result = safe_globals['check_func'](final_state)

        if not isinstance(result, bool):
            print("Function did not return a boolean. Result: {result}")
            return False, None, "Function did not return a boolean."

        return True, result, None
    except Exception as e:
        print("Error:", e)
        return False, None, str(e)
```

**Walkthrough.** Two things differ from the paper. First, the paper writes each check as $f_{c_k}(S_{final})$, a function of the final state only. The code also puts `initial_state` into the function's global scope, and the generation prompt tells the model to use it for checks like "has X been added" (X was missing before and exists now). So the checks really compare before and after, which is more expressive than the equation suggests. Second, despite the name `safe_globals`, the functions get the full Python builtins and run in the trainer's own process, so an LLM-written check could import modules or touch files. That is fine for a research release, but you would sandbox it before running untrusted generated code at scale. The same `exec` pattern (`init_env_class`, lines 7-21) loads the environment classes themselves.

### 3. One bad tool call ends the episode with zero reward

**Problem.** The agent's tool call is dispatched straight to a method of the generated class. What happens when that method raises an error?

`interact_with_env/envscaler_env/base_env.py:229-235 @ 96ae8b0`
```python
        except Exception:
            # Catch execution exception and terminate
            error_log = traceback.format_exc()
            observation = {"type": "user", "content": "Error: <Exception>\n" + error_log}
            terminated = True
            self._record_step(action, observation, terminated, reward)
            return observation, reward, terminated, truncated, info
```

**Walkthrough.** Tools are called as `getattr(self.env_instance, action['name'])(**action['arguments'])` (line 210). If the method raises anything, including the `TypeError` you get from passing a wrong argument name, the episode ends right there with `reward` still at its initial 0.0. The checklist is never run, so earlier correct work earns nothing. The paper does not describe this. It makes RL harsher than the partial-credit story suggests: a slip in argument names wipes out the whole episode. The code also cannot tell an agent mistake apart from a bug in the generated environment, and bugs remain likely, since type and attribute errors were the top failure types even among tested environments. The same happens when an episode runs out of steps: the RL manager marks it truncated and the reward is never computed (`rl/.../traj_env_manager_for_env_scaler.py:227-235`).

### 4. The environment quality filter counts "Warning" as passing

**Problem.** Turn 100 Pass/Warning/Fail verdicts into a keep-or-discard decision.

`skel_builder/stage3_check_env/step3_filter_env_by_check_result.py:38-48 @ 96ae8b0`
```python
def select_env(data, select_field, threshold):
    """Filter environments based on selected field and threshold."""
    new_data = []
    if select_field == "not_fail":
        # Filter by pass + warning rate
        for item in data:
            func_test_result_summary = item["func_test_result"]['func_test_cases']['summary']
            not_fail_acc = (func_test_result_summary["pass_count"]+ func_test_result_summary["warning_count"]) / func_test_result_summary["total_count"]
            if not_fail_acc >= threshold:
                new_data.append(item)
        return new_data
```

**Walkthrough.** The script's `__main__` calls `select_env(data, "not_fail", 0.85)`. So the 0.85 cut-off is applied to (Pass + Warning) / total, not to the Pass rate that Figure 3 and the $score_{env}$ equation suggest. The checking agent's prompt defines Warning as "the method works and meets functional expectations, but there are potential issues such as missing parameter validation, lack of boundary checks". Counting those as passing is a reasonable choice, but it means an environment can pass the filter with many weakly validated tools. Two more differences from the paper: the released rollout script defaults to `max_steps = 30` test rounds, not the 100 in the paper, and a round that raises an exception inside `run_step` is skipped with `continue` (`step2_roll_check.py:255-261`), which removes it from the count instead of recording it as a failure.

### 5. SFT scenarios have no check functions at all

**Problem.** Collecting 9K teacher trajectories is expensive. Does SFT data use the state-based reward to keep only correct trajectories?

`interact_with_env/envscaler_env/sft_non_conv_env_wo_reward_w_task_judge.py:1-6 @ 96ae8b0`
```python
"""
Non-conversational SFT environment with task judgment.
Compared to RL environment:
1. For cost efficiency, SFT tasks do not synthesize verification functions,
   trajectories are collected only through LLM self-judgment ("Task Failed") and format filtering.
"""
```

**Walkthrough.** No. SFT scenarios skip checklist generation to save cost. `interact_with_env/traj_filter.py` keeps a trajectory if its format is valid, its action count is between 3 and 29 (5 and 39 with a user), and it ends with the teacher declaring "Task Completed" (or the simulated user sending `###STOP###`). The teacher scores about 67/100 on these tasks, and nothing here removes trajectories where it claimed success but got the database wrong. So the SFT data probably includes a fair share of wrong-but-confident trajectories. The paper's Appendix B.2 does say it filters only on format and "judged by the LLM as impossible to complete", which matches, but the main text presents check functions as part of every scenario. The state-based reward is only used in RL (the 2.5K RL scenarios) and in the pilot study.

### 6. Hooking the reward into RL

**Problem.** Turn an episode into a training sample for ROLL.

`rl/roll/pipeline/agentic/env_manager/traj_env_manager_for_env_scaler.py:402-405 @ 96ae8b0`
```python
        # Calculate reward
        scores = [i['reward'] for i in self.rollout_cache.history]
        # Calculate episode total reward (sum of all steps' rewards)
        episode_score = sum(scores)
```

**Walkthrough.** Every step returns reward 0 except the final one, which carries the checklist score, so the sum is just the final score. Lines 441-444 then place that number on the last token of the joined multi-turn sequence, and every earlier token gets 0: one reward per trajectory, with no credit for individual steps. In the config (`rl/example/env_scaler/only_non_conv_qwen3_8gpu.yaml:148-150`), `reward_normalization` groups by `traj_group_id` with `mean_std`. Each score is normalized against the other 7 attempts at the same task, which is the group-baseline idea from GRPO, while the paper cites Reinforce++, whose title stresses *global* advantage normalization. Also, the validation set used during RL is `BFCLEval` (128 BFCL Multi-Turn Base samples, matching Figure 6b), which is one of the test benchmarks. The paper does not say how the final checkpoint was chosen. If it was picked using that curve, the BFCL numbers are slightly optimistic.

## Limitations, from the paper and from reading the code

The authors list these: everything is written by LLMs, so business logic and state design may drift from real systems; only closed, stateful domains (no web search or open information tasks); no latency, network failures or realistic error patterns; text only; and about 200 environments because of compute.

Worth adding from the evidence above:

- **The design favours shallow rules.** About 4.6 rules per environment, a "Modelability" score that favours simple single-class systems, and the weakest gains on τ-Bench, the most rule-heavy benchmark. Scaling the number of environments does not by itself scale rule depth.
- **Unvalidated reward code.** Checks are never tested against a known-correct or known-wrong final state. A check that is too loose rewards wrong behaviour, and one that is too strict is invisible noise. The paper's evidence that the checks work is indirect (stronger models score higher on 50 scenarios).
- **Harsh episode endings.** Any exception, including a bad argument name or a bug in the generated environment, ends the episode with 0. That may explain part of why small models are "more susceptible to noisy reward signals."
- **SFT data is not filtered for correctness**, as shown above.
- **One model family.** Every trained model is Qwen3, and the teacher is also Qwen3, so it is unclear how much of the gain comes from Qwen3-to-Qwen3 distillation.

## Where this sits in the vault

- The opposite approach, an LLM simulating the environment directly: [[2511.01824 - Simia Simulating Environments with Reasoning Models for Agent Training]].
- The field map this belongs to: [[2606.12191 - Agentic Environment Engineering Survey]].
- The conversation setting follows τ-bench: [[2406.12045 - Tau-Bench (Tool-Agent-User Interaction)]]. τ²-bench goes further with [[dual-control-environments]], where the user also has tools. EnvScaler's user has none.
- The reward design is an automated version of the verifier layer in [[four-layer-scoring-stack-for-rl-environments]], with the open risk from [[llm-generated-reward-programs-need-validation]].
- Checking outcomes rather than call syntax: [[execution-based-tool-evaluation]].
- Group-normalized RL mechanics: [[Cameron R. Wolfe - GRPO Tricks (Making RL Actually Work)]].

## Key claims

1. **Two-agent testing rejects about a quarter of generated environments.** 266 generated, 191 kept (28.2% rejected) at a 0.85 threshold over 100 test rounds, judged by GPT-4.1-mini / Qwen3-30B-A3B. (The released filter applies the threshold to Pass+Warning.)
   > From 266 synthetic environments, we selected 191, corresponding to a rejection rate of 28.2%.
   (Appendix C.2)
   > The number of test rounds N is set to 100, with a filtering threshold of 0.85. In total, we obtain 191 environments.
   (Section 3.4)

2. **SFT on synthetic environments improves all three benchmarks.** +8.67 BFCL-MT, +4.29 τ-Bench, +11.57 ACEBench-Agent, averaged over Qwen3-1.7B/4B/8B in thinking mode, with about 9K teacher trajectories from Qwen3-30B-A3B-Thinking on 140 environments.
   > Averaged across three models, BFCL-MT improves by 8.67 points, Tau-Bench by 4.29 points, and ACEBench-Agent by 11.57 points.
   (Section 5.2)

3. **RL after SFT adds more for the larger model.** Qwen3-8B gains +4.88 BFCL-MT and +3.46 τ-Bench from Reinforce++ on 51 held-out environments (64 tasks × 8 rollouts per step, up to 200 steps).
   > For example, Qwen3-8B achieves 4.88 and 3.46 point gains on BFCL-MT and Tau-Bench, respectively.
   (Section 5.2)

4. **Small models can get worse on rule-heavy tasks.** Qwen3-1.7B's τ-Bench Airline score drops from 16.00 to 14.00.
   > Qwen3-1.7B even slightly declines on the most challenging TauBench Airline task.
   (Section 5.2)

5. **Gains do not come from test-set look-alikes.** Qwen3-4B on BFCL-MT scores 32.00 when trained on the most similar half, 32.50 on the least similar half, and 31.25 on a random half (base 25.38). Similarity is measured by embedding topic and tool descriptions.
   > This suggests that the performance gains do not primarily depend on direct similarity between training and test environments, but on the problem-solving patterns and transferable tool-use skills learned from different environments.
   (Section 5.3, Table 5)

6. **More environments help, with the biggest jump early.** Qwen3-4B SFT on subsets from 0 to 141 environments, evaluated on BFCL-MT and ACEBench-Agent.
   > The most pronounced improvement occurs when scaling from 0 to 20 environments; although the rate of gain slows beyond this point, performance continues to rise overall.
   (Section 5.4, Figure 7)

7. **You cannot learn to handle a missing tool without examples of it.** Miss-Func stays flat (about 32-33) in every SFT setting for Qwen3-8B on BFCL-MT.
   > Performance on Miss-Func does not improve, primarily because the training data lacks samples with missing tool types.
   (Section 5.5, Table 6)

8. **SFT before RL beats RL alone overall.** Qwen3-8B direct RL: BFCL-MT 37.62, τ-Bench 42.30, ACEBench 63.05, against 41.88 / 44.81 / 72.50 for SFT+RL.
   > Besides, compared with “SFT + RL” in Table 4, the overall gains from direct RL remain limited, highlighting that SFT initialization is still important for better policy quality.
   (Section 5.6, Table 7)

9. **The synthetic tasks are hard and separate models.** On 50 Non-Conversation scenarios, the pilot scores range from 37.53 (4B, no thinking) to 67.07 (30B), with 69.38 for Qwen3-8B best-of-8.
   > Qwen3-8B (Thinking) scores 57.78, while Qwen3-4B (Non-Think) scores only 37.53.
   (Section 4.4, Table 3)

10. **Checking the final state accepts any valid solution path.** This is a design claim, not a measurement.
    > evaluation based on the environment’s final state is agnostic to the solution process and can accommodate multiple valid solution paths.
    (Section 4.2)

11. **Building environments is cheap.** About $1 per environment and $0.06 per scenario with GPT-4.1 and GPT-4.1-mini, most of it spent on the 100-round two-agent test.
    > Under the GPT-4.1/mini combination, the average cost per environment is about $1 and the cost per scenario is about $0.06.
    (Section 5.8, Table 8)

12. **Independent quality ratings are high.** Average scores above 8.5 out of 10 on tool-code match, correctness and robustness for all 191 environments, rated by Claude-4.5-Sonnet (which the authors say agrees closely with human judgment).
    > the 191 synthesized environments achieve high average scores of 8.5+ across all three dimensions.
    (Section 5.7, Figure 9)
